newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese firms keep cutting cross-shareholdings.
newsitem.headline: Japanese firms keep cutting cross-shareholdings.

text.p: Japanese firms continued selling off shares in each other last fiscal year, further unravelling one of the ties that has bound corporate Japan for decades.
Since the early 1990s, the risk of holding stocks long term has grown in Japan due to a fall in asset values after the collapse of its "bubble" of inflated stock and land prices.

Analysts say declining unrealised profits from shareholdings and slow growth in assets will continue, putting pressure on a web of interconnected stock holdings. Such holdings were aimed at maintaining close business ties, protecting firms from hostile takeovers and supporting overall stock prices.

Daiwa Institute of Research (DIR) analyst Masami Hamaguchi said the ratio of cross-shareholdings fell to 37.2 percent of listed shares in the year to March 31 from 37.8 percent a year earlier. In the heady bubble days of 1987 and 1988 the ratio was about 43 percent. "We see the cutting of the cross-shareholdings continuing for at least several years to come," Hamaguchi said.
Corporations want in particular to dump unnecessary bank stocks as their dependence on bank loans is diminishing now they are increasingly obtaining funds from capital markets.
"The 'Big Bang' financial reforms will probably accelerate such moves, as financial deregulation will give firms more opportunity to raise funds directly from the markets," he said.

DIR estimated that if listed Japanese firms cut banks they deal with to five from the current average of nine they could unload about five billion bank shares worth seven trillion yen ($60.8 billion). If they dealt with only three banks, 12 billion shares worth 11 trillion yen ($95.6 billion) could be sold.

Financial institutions themselves are trying to unload shares they hold in other financial institutions, partly to meet stricter capital adequacy standards. To increase return on investments, life insurers have also cut risky shareholdings.

But Nikko Research Center analyst Kouya Hasegawa said while big firms may be keen to cut cross-shareholdings with banks, small and medium-sized firms dependent on bank loans may want to cement ties with banks by interlocking shareholdings.

"I don't expect cross-shareholdings between companies and banks to decline rapidly," he said. While banks wanted to reduce holdings of risk assets such as shares in order to boost their capital adequacy ratios, they would not risk losing corporate clients by aggressively cutting cross-shareholdings, he said.

The biggest factors affecting cross-shareholdings are seen emerging in mid-1998, when a Finance Ministry panel finalises proposals on introducing mark-to-market accounting for firms' holdings of financial products such as stocks and derivatives.
In mark-to-market accounting the value of a position is calculated based on the daily closing price, thereby reflecting unrealised profit or loss on an outstanding position.

In Japan, financial products are fundamentally appraised according to their purchase cost, and gains or losses need to be posted only when positions are closed, regardless of the size of an open position a firm is holding.

Japan is expected to introduce mark-to-market accounting from fiscal 1999/00 as part of its Big Bang reforms, but from this fiscal year financial firms have been allowed to use the method for short-term financial-product trading accounts.

Japanese firms are sitting on massive unrealised profits on shares bought long ago at low prices. If these were appraised in balance sheets, the increase in asset value would erode the return on equity, analysts said.

They said if Japan decided to adopt mark-to-market accounting on shareholdings, the risk of securities price fluctuations affecting earnings would rise sharply and firms would be forced to sell off the holdings. ($1=115 yen)
